content: Hi everyone, really glad you could all make it today. My name's Claire, and I'll be leading the conversation. Before we get going — just a few quick things to mention. We're going to be talking for around 45 minutes, and the session is being recorded for research purposes, so if you could keep that in mind. Everything you say stays within the research team — nothing gets attributed to you by name. There are genuinely no right or wrong answers here. I'm not testing you, and I don't have a view on what the correct answer to any of these questions is. What I'm actually interested in is what you think, what you do, what you've noticed — real experiences, not what sounds reasonable or what you think I'm hoping to hear. It works best when it feels like a conversation between you rather than three separate interviews happening at the same time, so if something someone else says connects with your experience — or you think they've got it completely wrong — just jump in. You don't have to wait to be asked. Okay, let's start simply. What's your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.

Right, well for me it's got to be the pub, hasn't it. I mean, I've got a couple of regulars I go to in Manchester with the lads — we've been going to the same places for years now. There's just something about it, you know? You can talk, have a laugh, nobody's rushing you on. It's where we actually catch up properly.

I work during the week, some of the lads are scattered about, so the pub's just... it's the place where we all naturally end up. You sit down with a pint, nobody's checking their phone every five seconds, or at least not as much, and you can have a proper conversation. Or just sit in comfortable silence sometimes, which sounds daft but it's actually nice.

I've tried the whole going to the cinema or whatever with mates, but it's not the same — you're sat there not talking for two hours. With the pub you've got that flexibility. You can stay for one and leave, or you can be there all night if it's a good night. It feels... I don't know, normal? Like that's just what we do.

Yeah, I'd say the pub for me too, but it's... it's a bit different out here, I think. I mean, Gregor's right about it being the place where you naturally end up, but out in the village there isn't really anywhere else to go, is there? It's not so much a choice. There's the one pub, and that's it. You go there because what else are you going to do — drive twenty minutes to the next town? 

So it becomes less about picking somewhere nice and more just... necessary, I suppose. It's the default. But that said, he's spot on about what happens when you're actually there. Same thing — you sit down, have a pint, catch up properly with people you've known for years. The lads I see, we've all been coming to the same place forever.

The difference though is it serves a different function out here. It's not just a social spot, it's kind of the hub, you know? You bump into people, you hear what's going on in the village, it's where things get discussed. It's the only place people gather really. So it matters in a different way than maybe it does in the city where you've got options.

Yeah, that's a fair point actually. I hadn't thought of it like that. You're right — I do have options, don't I. I could go for a walk, I could go to a bar somewhere else, there's cinemas, restaurants, all sorts. So when I choose the pub it's because I genuinely want to be there, or it's where the lads have already decided we're going.

But what you're saying about it being the hub, the default place — that does change things. I mean, there's still a lot of the same feeling, the sitting down and having that time with people you know, but you're picking it, whereas it sounds like you're just... that's where you end up because that's where everyone goes anyway. 

I suppose that's probably why it works so well though. Like, when it's the only option people show up, and then it becomes this proper social thing rather than just somewhere to get a pint. There's probably more of a real community feel to that than what I get in Manchester, even if I think I'm choosing it.

Makes you wonder if having too many choices might actually change the dynamic a bit. I don't know. But yeah, fair dos — it's definitely different when you've actually got somewhere else you could be instead.

That's exactly it, yeah. When it's the only option, you commit to it differently. Everyone knows they'll be there on a Friday or Saturday, so you actually show up. You don't cancel because there's five other things you could do instead. And because everyone's in the same boat, there's this... I don't know, understanding between people maybe.

The bonds are different. Like, you're not just mates who decided to grab a pint — you're people who've all made the effort to be in the same room because that's where you meet. It creates something real. You know the landlord, you know everyone in there, you know their business. It's not anonymous like a big city pub probably is.

Gregor's right though that it's a different kind of choice. But I'd say the fact that it's inevitable, that there's nowhere else to go, it actually strengthens things rather than weakens them. Because you can't just drift away or pick somewhere trendier. You're stuck with the same place, the same people, year after year. That builds actual community, doesn't it? Not just friendships, but something bigger.

I mean, downside is if you fall out with someone or if the pub's not great, you've got no escape. But most of the time I reckon that limitation works in our favour. Forces you to make it work.
James, you're coming from a different setting to these two — what's your answer to that?

Yeah, well... I'd say the pub as well, but I'm sort of in the middle of what you two have going on, aren't I? Suburban down here in the South East, so we've got a bit more than Mark's got — there's a couple of pubs within driving distance, maybe a golf club — but nowhere near the range Gregor's talking about in Manchester.

I think what Mark said about it being the hub really resonates. I mean, I do have a choice in theory, but in practice? You end up at the same place because that's where the other lads are. It's just easier that way. Nobody has to negotiate it. You know where to find people.

But I'm not sure I'd say the limitation strengthens things, Mark. I think... I mean, yes, you get to know people properly. But I reckon a lot of it's just habit, isn't it? We go there because we've always gone there, and changing it would require effort nobody can be bothered with. That's not quite the same as building community deliberately.

Though saying that, I've known some of the blokes I see for thirty years now. So maybe it does work, whether it's by choice or by default. We just turn up and it's straightforward. No one's thinking too much about it.

Good stuff — so the pub comes up for all three of you, though with some real differences in what that actually means depending on where you are. Let's build on that a bit. How do you decide what to eat? Day to day — what goes into that?

Well, it's not complicated really, is it? I mean, I work full time, so most days it's whatever I can grab that doesn't take long. Bit of chicken, some veg, something quick. My wife does most of the cooking anyway, so I'm not thinking about it that much — whatever she's put on.

Weekends are different though. That's when I might actually think about it. We'll do a roast on Sunday, or we might go to that pub we were just talking about and get something there. But that's because we've got time and we're doing something social, aren't we? It's not just about the food, it's about the outing.

The thing is, I don't think people are choosing what to eat based on... I don't know, some grand plan. You look in the cupboard, you think about what doesn't take an hour to prepare because you're knackered, and you do that. Unless you're going out somewhere, and then it's a bit of an event. But day to day? It's pragmatic. You're not thinking much beyond getting fed.

Right, but I think it's different out here though. I mean, James, what you're saying about pragmatism — yeah, that's fair enough. But when you've only got certain things available, you're making decisions based on that constraint rather than just what's easiest or quickest.

Like, I can't just pop to Tesco or whatever if I fancy something specific. You go to the village shop, and they've got what they've got. So you're thinking about what's in season, what's actually available locally. You plan a bit more because you can't just nip out for ingredients. And that changes how you think about food, I reckon. You're working with what you've got rather than choosing from endless options.

But also — and this connects back to what we were saying earlier — there's something about that constraint that creates a different kind of commitment, doesn't it? Like the pub thing. You're not just grabbing whatever. You're part of a rhythm. Sunday roast because that's what you do. Eating what grows or what the local farm's got because that's what's there. It becomes less about convenience and more about... I don't know, being part of something seasonal, being tied to where you actually live.

James, you said habit isn't the same as building community deliberately. But maybe out here the two things are harder to separate. The habits ARE the community, because everyone's working within the same limits.

Fair point about the seasonal stuff, Mark. But I think you're... I don't know, maybe romanticizing it a bit? I mean, yeah, constraint changes things. But I'm not sure it automatically makes them better or more meaningful, does it?

I've got the local Tesco down the road and the farm shop, and I do go to both. I can choose. But I'm not thinking about it as being part of some bigger rhythm or community thing — I go to the farm shop because the veg is decent and it's on my way home sometimes. That's it. It's still pragmatic, just with a bit more choice.

The difference is I could drive to three different supermarkets if I wanted. I could order stuff online. I don't, mostly because it's easier not to bother. But that's different from you lot where you just... can't. You're making a virtue out of necessity, I reckon. Which fair enough, you've got to live there. But the constraint creating community — I'm not sure about that. You're all doing the same things because you don't have alternatives, not because you've chosen to be part of something together.

I mean, you probably do know each other better. But that might just be because it's a small village and you bump into the same people constantly, not because buying seasonal veg is somehow binding you to the community. Does that make sense? It's just... what you're stuck with.

No, I get what you're saying, but I think you're missing the point a bit. I'm not saying it's better or making some romantic thing out of it. I'm just saying it's different, and that difference matters.

You say you're not thinking about it as part of a bigger rhythm — but that's because you don't have to. You've got options. But when you haven't got options, it's not that you're making a virtue out of nothing. It's that the constraint actually shapes how you interact with things differently. Not better necessarily, just differently.

Like, you go to the farm shop because it's on your way home. Fair enough. But out here, I go to the village shop and I'm talking to people I know. The bloke who runs it knows what I usually get. In winter when stuff's scarce you're having conversations about what's available. That's not me romanticizing — that's just what happens when there's only one shop and you go there regularly.

And it's not that we're all doing the same things because we're stuck with no alternatives and that somehow binds us. It's that the constraint creates a different kind of social pattern. You can't avoid people. You see the same faces. You end up in the same pub. You shop in the same place. That builds familiarity whether you set out to build community or not.

So yeah, we're stuck with what we've got. But that stuckness actually does create something real. It's not virtue-making. It's just how it works out here. And I think that's worth noticing, rather than saying it's just necessity we're dressing up.

Right, okay. Yeah, I hear what you're saying actually. You're not wrong about that — the constraint does shape the pattern differently. I can see that. The shop owner knowing what you get, the conversations that happen because there's only one place to go. That's real. I wasn't saying it wasn't.

But here's the thing — I'm doing the same thing, just with a bit more choice built in. I've got my regular places. I know the bloke at my local shop, we chat about stuff. I see the same people down the pub most weeks. I see the same mates, we do the same things. It's just that if I wanted to go somewhere different, I could. But I don't, mostly, because the pattern's already there and it works.

So I'm not missing the point about how constraint shapes things. I get that. But I'm also not sure you're right that what you've got is something I can't have just because I've got options. The familiarity's still there. The pattern's still there. I'm still seeing the same people regularly, talking to people I know. It's just... less forced, maybe? Less inevitable?

I don't think having choice means I'm missing out on community or familiarity or whatever. It just means if the pattern wasn't working, I could change it. But it is working, so I don't. That's not the same as not having it.

That's a useful distinction actually — same pattern, less inevitability. I want to pick that thread up properly, because you've both been touching on something that feeds right into what I wanted to ask next. James, you mentioned earlier just looking in the cupboard and going from there. Mark, you talked about working with what's available seasonally. Gregor, we haven't heard from you yet on this — how do you decide what to eat day to day? What's actually driving it for you?

Right, yeah. I mean, honestly? It's a bit of a mix. During the week I'm working, so it's quick — chicken, pasta, whatever I can throw together in twenty minutes. I'm not thinking too hard about it. But I've got a bit more flexibility than James in that my wife works as well, so we kind of share it — sometimes I'll cook, sometimes she does, and we just sort of decide on the day based on what we fancy and what we've got in.

The difference I suppose is I can pop to Tesco when I need something, or if we fancy a specific meal we'll just get what we need. There's loads of choice. But to be honest, we probably go to the same couple of supermarkets most of the time anyway, and we've got our regular places we'll eat out at — like we'll go back to the same restaurants or pubs we know are decent.

So I'm not sure I'm that different from what you two are saying, really. I've got choice, yeah, but in practice I'm probably doing the same things most weeks. I'm not sitting there going right, let me explore every option available in Manchester. That would be exhausting. You settle into a rhythm because it's easier, innit. Whether that's because you've got to or because you can't be bothered to change it — I mean, the end result's probably pretty similar.

Yeah, but here's the thing though — I hear what you're both saying, but I think you might actually be talking past each other a bit.

Mark, you're saying the constraint creates something real, and James, you're saying you get the same familiarity anyway because you choose to stick with the pattern. And you're both right, aren't you? But I think the thing is... when it's forced, you can't just abandon it when it gets awkward or boring or whatever. You've got to make it work.

Whereas with me in Manchester, or James down south — if the local pub started getting rough, or the shop owner was a bit dodgy, or we just fancied a change... we could leave. We could go somewhere else. And maybe that does mean we're less committed, I don't know. But it also means the people we do keep showing up for, the places we do keep going back to — that's actually a choice we're making, isn't it?

I'm not saying that's better than what you've got, Mark. But it's different. I'm choosing to go back to my regulars because they're good. You've got to make it work because there's nowhere else to go. One's not automatically stronger than the other — they're just... different kinds of real.

Does that make sense? I'm not totally sure what I think about it, to be honest. But I don't reckon it's just about the constraint or just about convenience. It's both, depending on where you are.

Yeah, that's it exactly. That's what I was trying to get at. Gregor's nailed it.

Because Mark, you keep coming back to the constraint creating something real, and I'm not arguing it doesn't. But you're also suggesting that because I've got options, what I've got is somehow less solid or less committed. And that's not it at all.

I choose to go back to the same places. I choose to see the same people. That's deliberate. And yeah, if it went wrong — if the pub got dodgy or the bloke at the shop was a pain — I could go somewhere else. But I haven't needed to, because it works. That's not a weakness in what I've got. That's just... it's actually functioning properly.

I think there's a difference between being locked in and choosing to stay. You're locked in, Mark. You've made the best of it and fair play to you. But I'm not locked in. I'm choosing it. And I don't think that means my relationships or my patterns are any thinner than yours. They're just not constrained by geography in the same way.

Gregor's right — they're different kinds of real. Yours is forced to work. Mine is choosing to keep working. Neither one's automatically stronger.

That's a good place to leave that one — different kinds of real, as Gregor put it. I want to pull us back to food for a bit, because I think there's more there. Mark, you haven't said much yet about how you actually decide what to eat day to day — what does that look like for you?

Right, yeah. Well, day to day it's... it's pretty straightforward, really. I work during the week, so it's quick stuff mostly. Bit of mince, potatoes, veg. My wife cooks most nights, I'll do weekends sometimes. Nothing fancy.

But the thing is — and I think this is where it actually connects to what we've been saying — I can't just decide on the day that I fancy something and nip out to get it. If it's Tuesday night and I'm thinking pasta, I need to have the stuff at home already. So you plan ahead a bit. You think about what you're going to need for the week when you go to the shop. And because there's only the one shop, you go maybe once a week, sometimes less.

That's not me being romantic about it. That's just the reality. You've got to think ahead because you can't just pop out. So yeah, we eat what's there, what's in season at the farm if we get down there, what the shop's got. And because of that, you end up knowing what grows when, what's fresh when. Not because I've chosen to be all locavore or whatever — just because that's how it works when you can't get everything all year round.

It's practical. It's the only way it functions out here. But James and Gregor — they've both got the luxury of not having to think about it like that. They can decide on the day. I can't. That's the actual difference, isn't it. Not better or worse, just... you're working around a constraint I'm not.

Thanks Mark — so you've got the planning baked in by necessity, whereas Gregor and James are making it up a bit more on the day. That's a useful difference to have on the table. I want to move us on to something a bit different now. Thinking about everything you eat — the choices you make day to day — do you think being a man has anything to do with it? Does your gender shape what you eat, or not really?

Hmm. I mean... yeah, probably does, doesn't it? Though I hadn't really thought about it before you asked.

Like, my wife — she's the one doing most of the cooking during the week. I help out at weekends, but that's sort of the arrangement we've fallen into. And I'm not thinking about nutrition or whether we're getting our five a day or anything like that. I just... eat what's there. She's the one who's got that in her head, I think. Whether we need more veg, whether we've had too much red meat that week, all that.

So in that sense, yeah, being a bloke probably means I'm not thinking about the food side of things as much as she is. It's one of those things where you just accept it, don't you — she cooks, I'll do the washing up or whatever. And I'm not saying that's right or wrong, it's just... that's what we do.

But the other side of it is I don't feel like I'm restricted in what I eat because I'm a man, if that makes sense? Like, I'm not avoiding things or only eating certain things. It's just that I'm not the one organising it, planning it, thinking ahead about what we need. That bit's fallen to her.

I suppose if I was more into cooking I might think differently about it. But I'm not, so I don't really notice it day to day. It's just how it works for us.

Gregor's drawn that distinction between who's *thinking* about the food versus who's eating it — the planning, the nutrition, all of that falling to his wife while he just gets on with eating. Does that ring true for James and Mark, or does it work differently in your households?

Yeah, it rings true in terms of my wife doing most of the planning, but... I think it's a bit different for me, actually. Not in a way that's better or anything, but different.

Because I'm here during the day more often — I'm not commuting into an office like you lot — I end up seeing more of what goes into it. Like, I'll be at the shop and I'll talk to the bloke about what's available, what's coming in next week. I'll notice that the seasonal stuff's changed. And because there's only one shop, I'm kind of aware of the whole picture more. My wife does the planning, yeah, but I'm not just... eating what's there without thinking about it.

I mean, I'm not sat there working out the nutrition like she is, that's fair. But I'm more clued in to the constraints and the rhythms because I live with them day to day. Whereas Gregor, he's just accepting it without really thinking about whether it's... I don't know, whether it's something worth thinking about.

It's one of those things, isn't it. You fall into an arrangement and then you don't question it. My wife handles the planning, I help out when I'm needed. But because I'm here and I can see what's involved, I'm at least aware it's happening. I don't think I could just say "I don't notice it day to day" like Gregor does, because I do. It's there.

Fair point, I hear what you're saying. But I don't think I'm not noticing it or not thinking about it — I'm just not... I dunno, I'm not pretending it's some big revelation, am I?

I know my wife does the planning. I know that's part of how our household runs. I'm not oblivious to it. It's just that when you ask me what drives my food choices day to day, the honest answer is — I look in the fridge, I eat what's there. That's my bit of it. The planning bit, that's hers. And I accept that's how we do it.

But you're right that I'm probably less aware of the constraints than you are, Mark. Because I *can* just pop to Tesco, the choice is there somewhere in the background even if I'm not using it every day. Whereas you're dealing with the actual limit the whole time — you're at the shop, you're talking to the bloke, you're seeing what's available. So yeah, you've got a different awareness of it.

But I don't think that means I need to sit around questioning whether the arrangement I've got is something worth thinking about. It works. She does the planning, I eat the food, we're fed. That's not ignorance, that's just... how it is. I'm not saying it couldn't be different, but it isn't, so I'm not going to pretend it bothers me when it doesn't.

Yeah, but that's the thing though — you're saying it works, and fair enough, it probably does. But you're also saying you don't need to think about it, and I'm not sure those are the same thing.

Like, I'm not saying you should be bothered by it or that it's wrong. I'm saying that when you live with the constraint, you can't help but think about it. It's not optional. And I reckon that awareness — even if you're not sitting around questioning it — that's actually worth something.

You can just accept it without thinking because you've got the option to do something else if you wanted to. I can't. So I'm aware of it whether I like it or not. And I think there's a difference between accepting something because you've chosen to stick with it, and accepting it because you've got no choice but to make it work.

I'm not saying one's better, Gregor. But you're sliding past the difference a bit. You keep saying it works and you're not bothered, but that doesn't mean the awareness isn't there for me in a way it might not be for you. You can compartmentalize it — she does that bit, you do that bit. I can't, because the whole thing's interconnected out here. The shop, the seasons, what's available, who does what — it's all part of the same thing because there's nowhere else to go.

So yeah, you're aware it happens. But I'm aware of the whole system because I have to be. That's the actual difference.
James, you've been listening to these two go back and forth — where do you land on all this?

I'm... I'm actually with Gregor on this one, to be honest.

I mean, I hear what Mark's saying about the constraint forcing awareness, and yeah, I get that. But I think he's conflating two different things. One is the awareness of constraint — and yeah, he's got that, he lives with it. But the other is some kind of moral awareness about gender roles or how household arrangements work, and I'm not sure that actually follows from living in a village.

Mark's making it sound like because he can see the shop and he knows what's in season, he's got some deeper understanding of the system. But my wife does the planning too. And I'm not sitting around ignoring it — I know it's happening. I just don't think I need to be constantly aware of every constraint or limitation for that to be true.

Like, Mark, you can't just nip to Tesco — fine. But that doesn't mean your awareness of the gender dynamics in your household is sharper than Gregor's or mine. We might just be... accepting it without needing to think about it too hard. That's not the same as not being aware it exists.

I think you're trying to make a point about something bigger — maybe about choice and constraint and awareness — but I'm not sure it actually lands when you're talking about food shopping and who cooks what. That's just... household arrangements. They work or they don't.

So there's something interesting in what all three of you have said — you each describe a similar arrangement at home, wife does the planning, you eat what's there, but you're drawing different conclusions about what that means or whether it needs thinking about. Let me move us on, because I want to get into something related. Imagine you actually decided to go plant-based — not just cutting back, but a proper shift. What would need to change in your life for that to actually happen?

Well, that's straightforward isn't it — my wife would have to decide to do it. That's the reality.

I mean, she does the planning, she does most of the cooking. So if we went plant-based, she'd be the one figuring out what that means, what we need to get, how to make it work. And honestly, I don't think she'd want to. She's not interested in that sort of thing.

So it wouldn't actually happen unless she was on board with it. I'm not going to suddenly start doing all the meal planning myself just because I've decided I want to eat differently. That's... that's not how it works in our house.

I mean, I could do it if I was really bothered about it. Cook my own meals, sort my own stuff. But we're talking about a fundamental shift in how we eat as a household, aren't we? That requires buy-in from whoever's actually doing the work. And that's her.

So yeah — what would need to change? She'd need to think it was a good idea. That's the bit that matters. Everything else kind of flows from that.

So James is saying it comes down to his wife being on board — because she's the one who'd actually have to make it work. Does that land for you two, or does it look different from where you're sitting?

Yeah, it lands for me too, actually. Same situation — my wife does the planning, so if we were going to shift to something like that, she'd need to be the one thinking it through. Because she's the one who knows what we've got, what we need, what works.

But here's what I'm getting at, right — and this is exactly what I've been trying to say. James just said he *could* do it himself if he was really bothered. Cook his own meals, sort his own stuff. He's got that option. If he decided tomorrow that he wanted to go plant-based, he could. He'd pop to Tesco, get what he needs, make it happen. It would be a hassle, sure, but he could do it.

I couldn't, not in the same way. There's only one shop. If my wife's not on board, I'm eating what she's planning. I could try to do my own thing, but where am I getting the stuff? I'm going to the same shop, having to explain to the bloke why I'm buying different things, and I'm probably making life more complicated for the person who's handling the rest of it.

So yeah, James's wife would need to be on board. But James has got the choice to step up and handle it himself if he wanted to badly enough. I haven't got that same option because of where I live. And that's not about being aware of constraint — that's about what's actually possible. That's the difference I've been trying to say.
Gregor, you're in a similar spot to James on the household side — she does the planning — but you've got the shops around you. Does Mark's distinction ring true from where you're sitting?

Yeah, I mean... Mark's got a point, hasn't he? If I decided tomorrow I wanted to go plant-based, I could actually do it. I could go to Tesco, get what I need, figure it out myself if my wife wasn't interested. It would be a pain, but I could.

Mark couldn't do that in the same way. He's stuck with what's available locally, and if his wife's not on board, he's genuinely limited in what he can actually pull off. That's real.

But I think — and I don't want to keep going in circles here — but I think the question is whether I would actually do that, you know? Like, yeah, I've got the option. But would I bother? Probably not. I'd have a conversation with my wife about it, and if she wasn't keen, that would be that. I'm not going to start doing all my own meal planning just because I've got the theoretical choice to.

So Mark's right that I've got more options. But I'm not sure that automatically means I'm in a better position to make a shift like that, because I'm probably not going to use those options anyway. I'd still need her to be on board, really. The difference is I *could* do something about it on my own if I really wanted to, whereas Mark genuinely can't.

So yeah, his point stands. I've got the freedom to do it if I got desperate enough. He hasn't. That's a real difference in what's actually possible for us.

Gregor, I want to pick up on something, because you said something earlier — back when we were on gender — that you don't feel restricted in what you eat because you're a man. And now you're saying: yeah, I've got the freedom to go plant-based on my own, but I probably wouldn't bother, I'd need my wife to be on board. I'm curious about the relationship between those two things. Is 'not feeling restricted' the same as 'having the option'? Or is something else going on there?

Right, okay. That's... yeah, that's a fair question actually.

I think there's a difference between not feeling restricted by what I eat — like, I'm not avoiding things or only eating certain things because I'm a man — and then the whole arrangement of who does what in the household. Those are two different things, aren't they?

Like, I can eat whatever I want when it's put in front of me. Nobody's saying that's not for blokes or whatever. That's not restricted. But the fact that my wife's doing the planning and I'm just eating what's there — that's a different thing. That's not about restriction on me, that's just... how the household runs.

But you're right, I suppose, that if I actually wanted to change things — go plant-based, change the whole way we eat — I'd probably need her to do the work. And I'm not sure that's not a restriction, actually. It's just a different kind. It's not that I can't eat certain things. It's that I'm kind of... dependent on her to make changes to the system, even though I've got the option to do it myself if I really wanted to badly enough.
